name: Lilau
confidence_why: Capell 1952, the only first-hand description of Lilau, places stress on either the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable, and Vormann and Scharfenberger 1914 report the same penult-dominant window for the sister dialect Monumbo, with nothing published contradicting either.

catalog_quote: The plosive elements in ts, dz are slight. In Lilau I did not record them, only s (not z). Syllables can be closed in M., but in L. the only consonant clusters found are those with homorganic nasals. There are no semantic tones. Stress rests on either the penultimate or antepenultimate syllables in each dialect. Lilau preserves fuller forms, where the words are at all comparable, e.g. spear, M. kindar, L. kindara; banana, M. kuan, L. kuani; tree, M. ka, L. kaja.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Capell (who recorded Lilau himself) says stress falls on the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable, in both Monumbo and Lilau, and that there are no lexical tones; he gives no conditioning for the choice. The only fuller source, the 1914 Monumbo grammar (Vormann & Scharfenberger, p. 3, Monumbo proper, saved as, p. 17), says the accent rests predominantly on the penultimate syllable, especially in the plural, less often on the antepenultimate, and shifts in compounds: 'Der Akzent ruht vorwiegend auf der vorletzten Silbe. namentlich im Plural, weniger häufig auf der drittletzten Silbe. In zusammengesetzten Formen wird der Akzent verschoben, so akú-atá = akunáta mein Vater, mér-kurún = mérkurun Knabe, kéatsak-kurún = keátkurun Mädchen.' (= The accent rests predominantly on the penultimate syllable, especially in the plural, less often on the antepenultimate. In compound forms the accent is shifted, e.g..). Provisional reading: penultimate-dominant with unconditioned antepenultimate cases; 'unclear or contradictory' would be the alternative reading if Capell's sentence is taken alone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in either source. The 1914 grammar (p. 2) adds only that in diphthongs the first element takes the stress ('Bei den Diphthongen erhält in der Regel der erste Laut die Betonung').
new_statements.exceptions: Capell: antepenultimate stress occurs alongside penultimate, no rule given. Vormann & Scharfenberger (Monumbo): antepenult 'weniger häufig'; accent shifts in compounds (akú-atá > akunáta 'my father', mér-kurún > mérkurun 'boy', kéatsak-kurún > keátkurun 'girl').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from elicited citation forms and short sentences; Capell's Lilau material is a phoneme chart, grammatical notes, a text and a wordlist gathered from Lilau villagers, with Monumbo forms taken from the 1914 grammar. No instrumental or text-based study exists; the 1914 grammar marks accent on cited forms throughout but describes Monumbo, not Lilau.
new_statements.identity_note: Capell's statement is made jointly for "each dialect" of the Monumbo-Lilau pair: Monumbo (M., ISO mxk; data taken from Vormann & Scharfenberger 1914) and Lilau (L., lila1246; Capell's own notes "taken by the present writer from natives of Lilau village", which he places inside the Ngaimbom dialect area). The supporting 1914 grammar's accent rule (p. 3) is for Monumbo proper; that book treats the Ngaimbom (= Lilau) as speakers of "einen Dialekt des Monumbo" (p. 1) but gives no Lilau-specific data. Later authors (Z'graggen 1971: 64% shared cognates; Laycock 1975) regard Monumbo and Lilau as separate languages.
